screens.title: Remote Access vs. Site-to-Site VPNs
screens.narratorSegment: Let's begin by clarifying the core concept of remote access VPNs and how they differ from site-to-site VPNs. Remote access VPNs are designed for individual users who need to securely connect to a corporate network from outside the office, whether they're working from home, a coffee shop, or traveling. Think of it as creating a secure, encrypted tunnel from a single client device directly to the corporate network. This allows the remote user to access internal resources like applications, file shares, or internal websites, just as if they were physically connected to the office LAN. The primary benefits are increased workforce mobility, enhanced security for remote workers by encrypting their traffic over untrusted public networks, and ensuring compliance with data protection regulations. In contrast, site-to-site VPNs connect entire networks, such as a branch office to a headquarters, creating a permanent, secure link between two distinct locations. A common misconception is that these VPN types are interchangeable; however, their design and purpose are quite distinct, catering to different connectivity needs. Remote access focuses on individual user security and flexibility, while site-to-site focuses on network-to-network connectivity.

Module 6›Chapter 6.6›Remote Access VPNs
Core Concept

Remote Access vs. Site-to-Site VPNs

Understanding the fundamental differences and use cases.

Remote Access VPN

  • Connects individual remote users.
  • Client-to-network tunnel.
  • Ideal for mobile workforce.

Site-to-Site VPN

  • Connects entire networks.
  • Network-to-network tunnel.
  • Ideal for branch office connectivity.
Example Scenario

A sales representative working from a hotel needs to access the company's CRM system. A Remote Access VPN is the perfect solution, establishing a secure tunnel from their laptop to the corporate network. In contrast, connecting a new branch office to the main headquarters would require a Site-to-Site VPN.

Key Takeaway

Remote Access VPNs enable secure, flexible connectivity for individual users, while Site-to-Site VPNs link entire networks.

screens.title: SSL VPN vs. IPsec IKEv2 for AnyConnect
screens.narratorSegment: Cisco AnyConnect supports two primary VPN protocols for remote access: SSL VPN and IPsec IKEv2 VPN. Understanding their differences is key to choosing the right solution for your network. SSL VPNs, which actually utilize Transport Layer Security or TLS, the modern successor to SSL, are highly flexible because they leverage standard web protocols, specifically TCP port 443. This makes them exceptionally easy to traverse firewalls and Network Address Translation, or NAT, devices, as most networks already allow outbound web traffic. This ease of deployment is a significant advantage, especially for users connecting from diverse and potentially restrictive network environments. On the other hand, IPsec IKEv2 VPNs offer robust security and are often preferred for their superior performance and native operating system integration. However, they might require specific port allowances, typically UDP 500 and UDP 4500, which can sometimes be blocked by firewalls. A common misconception is that SSL VPN is less secure than IPsec; however, modern TLS implementations provide strong encryption. The choice often comes down to balancing ease of access with performance requirements and the specific network environment of your remote users. For instance, if you have many users connecting from public Wi-Fi networks with strict firewalls, SSL VPN might be more reliable.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.6›VPN Protocols
VPN Protocols

SSL VPN vs. IPsec IKEv2 for AnyConnect

Choosing the right protocol for remote access.

SSL VPN (TLS)

  • Uses standard web protocols (TCP 443).
  • Highly flexible, easy to traverse firewalls/NAT.
  • Good for diverse network environments.

IPsec IKEv2 VPN

  • Uses UDP ports 500, 4500.
  • Robust security and often better performance.
  • May require specific firewall allowances.
Real-World Connection

When designing a remote access solution, consider your users' typical connection environments. If many users connect from public Wi-Fi or home networks with restrictive firewalls, SSL VPN's ability to use TCP 443 makes it a more reliable choice. For internal corporate laptops with controlled network access, IPsec IKEv2 might be preferred for its performance benefits.

Key Takeaway

SSL VPN (TLS) offers high flexibility by using TCP 443, making it firewall-friendly, while IPsec IKEv2 provides robust security and performance, though it may require specific port allowances.

Protocol Comparison

VPN Protocols
SSL VPN (TLS)
  • TCP 443
  • Firewall-friendly
IPsec IKEv2

  • High performance

screens.title: AnyConnect SSL VPN Configuration Overview
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring a basic AnyConnect SSL VPN on a Cisco IOS-XE router involves a structured series of steps to ensure secure and functional remote access. First, you need to enable the webvpn feature on the router, which is the foundational command that activates the necessary services. Next, a critical step is to configure an SSL trustpoint for the router's identity certificate. This certificate is essential because it authenticates the VPN server to the client and encrypts the SSL/TLS control channel, ensuring that clients are connecting to a legitimate server and that their communication is private. Obtaining and installing a valid certificate, either from a public Certificate Authority or an internal Public Key Infrastructure, is a prerequisite for this step. Then, you define a webvpn gateway, which specifies the external interface IP address that clients will connect to and associates it with the SSL trustpoint you just configured. Following this, you create a webvpn context, or webvpn group on older IOS versions. This context defines all the specific VPN parameters for a group of users, such as the IP address pool from which clients will receive their IP addresses, the DNS servers they should use, and the authentication method. Finally, you associate this context with the gateway and apply the webvpn command to the external interface, bringing the entire service online. Each step builds upon the previous one, creating a robust and secure remote access solution.

screens.title: Configuring SSL Trustpoint and Gateway
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the initial configuration steps on a Cisco IOS-XE router, focusing on setting up the SSL trustpoint and the webvpn gateway. The SSL trustpoint is crucial because it defines the identity certificate that the router will present to AnyConnect clients. This certificate verifies the server's authenticity and encrypts the initial control channel, preventing man-in-the-middle attacks. You'll typically obtain this certificate from a trusted Certificate Authority, or generate a self-signed one for lab environments. Once the certificate is installed, you configure the crypto pki trustpoint and associate it with the certificate. Next, we define the webvpn gateway. This command specifies the external IP address and port that remote users will connect to, and it links this connection point to the SSL trustpoint. For example, if your router's public IP is 198.51.100.1, you'll configure the gateway to listen on this address, typically on port 443 for SSL VPN. It's vital that the hostname configured in the gateway matches the Common Name, or CN, on your SSL certificate to avoid certificate validation errors on the client side. These steps lay the secure foundation for all subsequent AnyConnect connections.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.6›CLI Walkthrough
CLI Walkthrough

Configuring SSL Trustpoint and Gateway

Essential steps for server identity and external access.

Configuration Snippets

! Assume a valid identity certificate (e.g., from a CA) is installed as 'MY_ROUTER_CERT'
! crypto pki trustpoint MY_TRUSTPOINT
!  enrollment terminal
!  revocation-check crl
!  exit
! crypto pki enroll MY_TRUSTPOINT

! Define IP Address Pool for VPN Clients
ip local pool VPN_POOL 172.16.100.1-172.16.100.254

! Enable WebVPN and define Gateway
webvpn gateway MY_WEBVPN_GATEWAY
 hostname router.cohortia.com
 ip address 198.51.100.1 port 443
 ssl trustpoint MY_TRUSTPOINT
 inservice
  • The `ssl trustpoint` command links the gateway to the router's identity certificate.
  • `hostname` in the gateway must match the certificate's Common Name (CN).
Key Takeaway

Properly configuring the SSL trustpoint and webvpn gateway ensures secure server identity and establishes the public entry point for AnyConnect clients.

Gateway & Trustpoint Relationship

Secure Connection
SSL Trustpoint (Certificate)
WebVPN Gateway (Public IP)
AnyConnect Client

screens.title: Configuring WebVPN Context and IP Pool
screens.narratorSegment: After setting up the SSL trustpoint and webvpn gateway, the next crucial step is to configure the webvpn context. This context, sometimes referred to as a webvpn group on older IOS versions, is where you define the specific VPN parameters that will apply to a group of remote users. Within this context, you'll specify the IP address pool from which AnyConnect clients will receive their IP addresses upon connecting. This ensures that each client gets a unique, routable IP within your corporate network. For example, you might define a pool like 172.16.100.1 to 172.16.100.254. You also configure DNS servers that clients should use, which is essential for resolving internal hostnames. Furthermore, this is where you define the authentication method, which we'll cover in more detail shortly. A key feature configured here is split tunneling. Split tunneling determines whether all client traffic goes through the VPN tunnel, known as full tunneling, or if only traffic destined for the corporate network goes through the tunnel, while other internet traffic bypasses it. This is configured using svc split-tunnel include or exclude commands. For instance, you might include your internal subnets like 192.168.1.0/24 and 10.0.0.0/24. Finally, you associate this context with the previously defined gateway and enable the webvpn feature on the external interface, bringing the entire AnyConnect service to life. This detailed configuration ensures that clients receive the correct network settings and access policies.

keyIdea.text: The webvpn context defines IP address pools, DNS settings, authentication, and split tunneling policies for groups of AnyConnect users.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.6›CLI Walkthrough
CLI Walkthrough

Configuring WebVPN Context and IP Pool

Defining user-specific VPN parameters and network access.

WebVPN Context Configuration

! Define WebVPN Context (for a group of users)
webvpn context MY_ANYCONNECT_CONTEXT
 gateway MY_WEBVPN_GATEWAY
 ssl authenticate verify all
 policy group MY_GROUP_POLICY
  functions svc-enabled
  svc address-pool VPN_POOL
  svc keep-client-installed
  svc dns-server 8.8.8.8 primary
  svc split-tunnel include 192.168.1.0 255.255.255.0
  svc split-tunnel include 10.0.0.0 255.255.255.0
  authentication aaa console
  exit
 default-group-policy MY_GROUP_POLICY
 inservice

! Apply WebVPN to the external interface
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 198.51.100.1 255.255.255.0
 webvpn
  • `svc address-pool` assigns IP addresses to connected clients.
  • `svc split-tunnel include` defines which traffic goes through the VPN.
Key Takeaway

The webvpn context is central to defining client IP addressing, DNS, authentication, and critical split tunneling policies for remote users.

WebVPN Context Parameters

screens.title: User Authentication Methods for AnyConnect
screens.narratorSegment: User authentication is a critical component of any remote access VPN solution, and Cisco AnyConnect offers a variety of robust methods to secure client access. The simplest method is using a local database, where usernames and passwords are configured directly on the VPN headend device. This is straightforward for small deployments, but it doesn't scale well for larger organizations due to the administrative overhead of managing credentials on multiple devices. For enterprise-level deployments, RADIUS, or Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service, is the most common and scalable method. RADIUS is a centralized authentication, authorization, and accounting protocol. The VPN headend forwards user credentials to a RADIUS server, such as Cisco ISE or Microsoft NPS, which then authenticates the user and sends back authorization attributes. This method is highly flexible and supports multi-factor authentication, or MFA, which is a crucial security layer today. TACACS+, or Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus, is similar to RADIUS but separates AAA functions and is often preferred for device administration rather than remote access. Finally, digital certificates offer strong, password-less authentication, often combined with a username and password for a robust two-factor authentication scheme. Choosing the right method depends on your organization's size, security requirements, and existing infrastructure. For example, a small business might start with a local database, but a large corporation would almost certainly leverage RADIUS with MFA.

screens.title: Configuring RADIUS and Local Authentication
screens.narratorSegment: Now, let's look at how to configure both RADIUS and local authentication methods on your Cisco IOS-XE router for AnyConnect VPNs. For RADIUS authentication, you first need to enable the AAA new-model, which is a foundational command for advanced authentication, authorization, and accounting services. Then, you define your RADIUS server group and specify the IP addresses of your RADIUS servers, along with a shared secret key that must match the configuration on the RADIUS server itself. This shared secret is crucial for secure communication between the router and the RADIUS server. Once the server group is defined, you'll configure the authentication method within the webvpn context or group-policy by specifying authentication-server-group followed by your RADIUS group name. This tells the VPN headend to forward authentication requests to the RADIUS server. For local authentication, which is simpler and suitable for smaller deployments, you just configure a username and password directly on the router using the username password command. Then, within the webvpn context, you specify authentication local. It's important to understand that while local authentication is quick to set up, RADIUS offers far greater scalability, centralized management, and support for advanced features like multi-factor authentication, making it the preferred choice for most enterprise environments. For example, if you have hundreds of remote users, managing their credentials on a central RADIUS server is much more efficient than on individual VPN devices.

Module 6›Chapter 6.6›CLI Walkthrough
CLI Walkthrough

Configuring RADIUS and Local Authentication

Implementing centralized and local user authentication.

Authentication Configuration Snippets

! Define AAA for RADIUS (if used)
aaa new-model
aaa authentication login default group radius local
aaa authorization network default group radius
radius server COHORTIA_RADIUS
 address ipv4 192.168.10.10 auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813
 key CohortiaRadiusKey!

! For local authentication (within webvpn context)
username cohortia password Cisco123!
! ... inside webvpn context MY_ANYCONNECT_CONTEXT ...
!  authentication aaa console  (defaults to local if no AAA server configured)
  • `aaa new-model` is required for advanced AAA services like RADIUS.
  • The `key` for the RADIUS server must match the shared secret on the RADIUS server.
Pro Tip

Always test your RADIUS configuration thoroughly after implementation. Use `debug aaa authentication` to monitor the authentication process and identify any issues with server reachability or shared secret mismatches. This proactive testing can save significant troubleshooting time later.

Key Takeaway

RADIUS provides scalable, centralized authentication for AnyConnect, configured via AAA and server groups, while local authentication offers a simpler, device-specific option for smaller deployments.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Common AnyConnect VPN Issues
screens.narratorSegment: Even with careful configuration, issues can arise with AnyConnect VPNs. Effective troubleshooting starts with understanding common problem areas and using the right tools. Begin by checking the AnyConnect client logs, which are an invaluable first resource for error messages related to connectivity, certificate validation, or authentication failures. These logs often provide clear indications of what went wrong. On the VPN headend, commands like show webvpn session all give you an overview of active and disconnected sessions, while show webvpn context provides detailed information specific to a configured VPN context. For deeper authentication issues, debug aaa authentication can reveal problems with RADIUS or TACACS+ communication, and debug webvpn anyconnect offers insights into the SSL VPN negotiation process. Common problems include certificate issues, such as mismatched common names, expired certificates, or untrusted Certificate Authorities, which prevent the SSL negotiation from completing. Authentication failures are also frequent, often due to incorrect usernames or passwords, unreachable RADIUS servers, or misconfigured shared secrets. IP address pool exhaustion can occur if the assigned pool runs out of available addresses, preventing new clients from connecting. Finally, firewall or Access Control List issues might block the necessary ports, TCP 443 for SSL VPN or UDP 500/4500 for IPsec IKEv2. Misconfigured split tunneling can also lead to unexpected network access behavior. For example, if a user can connect but can't reach internal resources, check the split tunneling configuration to ensure the correct subnets are included in the tunnel. By systematically checking these areas, you can efficiently diagnose and resolve most AnyConnect VPN problems.

Module 6›Chapter 6.6›Troubleshooting
Troubleshooting Guide

Troubleshooting Common AnyConnect VPN Issues

Diagnosing and resolving connectivity and authentication problems.

Common Issues & Solutions

  • Certificate Issues: Mismatched CN, expired certs, untrusted CAs. Ensure CN matches public IP/DNS.
  • Authentication Failures: Incorrect credentials, unreachable RADIUS, shared secret mismatch.
  • IP Pool Exhaustion: VPN client pool runs out of addresses. Expand the pool or reduce session timeouts.
  • Firewall/ACL Issues: Blocked TCP 443 (SSL VPN) or UDP 500/4500 (IPsec IKEv2).
Key Takeaway

Effective AnyConnect troubleshooting relies on systematic checks of client logs, headend status, debug outputs, and common problem areas like certificates, authentication, and network access rules.

Troubleshooting Flow

Troubleshooting Steps
1. Check Client Logs
2. Verify Headend Status
3. Use Debug Commands
4. Address Common Issues

Welcome to this masterclass on Remote Access VPNs with Cisco AnyConnect. In today's distributed work environment, providing secure and reliable access to corporate resources for remote users is paramount. This chapter will equip you with the knowledge to understand, configure, and troubleshoot Cisco AnyConnect, a leading solution for secure mobility. You'll learn how to differentiate remote access VPNs from other VPN types, delve into the architecture of the AnyConnect client, and master the configuration steps on Cisco IOS-XE routers. We'll also explore various authentication methods and essential troubleshooting techniques to ensure your remote workforce stays connected and protected. By the end of this session, you'll have a comprehensive understanding of how to implement and manage secure remote access solutions, enhancing both productivity and security for your organization. Secure Remote Access with Cisco AnyConnect means cisco anyconnect provides secure vpn access and a suite of endpoint security features for a mobile workforce.. In practical terms, empowering your workforce with flexible and protected connectivity. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

In this section, we'll outline the key skills and knowledge you'll gain. First, you'll be able to clearly explain the concept and significant benefits of remote access VPNs, understanding how they differ fundamentally from site-to-site VPNs. This distinction is crucial for selecting the right VPN solution for various organizational needs. For example, you'll know why a remote sales team needs remote access VPNs, while two branch offices require a site-to-site solution. Secondly, you will be able to describe the comprehensive architecture and various components of the Cisco AnyConnect Secure Mobility Client. This includes understanding its role not just as a VPN client, but as a unified security agent that provides a secure endpoint experience, offering features beyond just tunnel establishment. This foundational knowledge will prepare you for practical implementation and troubleshooting.

Continuing our objectives, you will learn to configure a basic Cisco AnyConnect SSL VPN on a Cisco IOS-XE router or an ASA. This hands-on skill is fundamental for establishing secure remote access. We'll walk through the necessary commands and concepts, such as setting up trustpoints and defining VPN parameters, so you can confidently implement a functional VPN solution. Furthermore, you will be able to implement robust user authentication for AnyConnect VPNs using various methods, including local databases, RADIUS, or TACACS+. Understanding these options allows you to choose the most secure and scalable authentication strategy for your network. Finally, you'll gain the ability to troubleshoot common AnyConnect client connectivity and authentication issues, a critical skill for maintaining network uptime and user productivity. This includes diagnosing certificate problems, authentication failures, and IP address pool exhaustion, ensuring you can quickly resolve real-world challenges.

Let's begin by clarifying the core concept of remote access VPNs and how they differ from site-to-site VPNs. Remote access VPNs are designed for individual users who need to securely connect to a corporate network from outside the office, whether they're working from home, a coffee shop, or traveling. Think of it as creating a secure, encrypted tunnel from a single client device directly to the corporate network. This allows the remote user to access internal resources like applications, file shares, or internal websites, just as if they were physically connected to the office LAN. The primary benefits are increased workforce mobility, enhanced security for remote workers by encrypting their traffic over untrusted public networks, and ensuring compliance with data protection regulations. In contrast, site-to-site VPNs connect entire networks, such as a branch office to a headquarters, creating a permanent, secure link between two distinct locations. A common misconception is that these VPN types are interchangeable; however, their design and purpose are quite distinct, catering to different connectivity needs. Remote access focuses on individual user security and flexibility, while site-to-site focuses on network-to-network connectivity.

Now, let's dive into Cisco AnyConnect Secure Mobility Client, which is far more than just a simple VPN client. It's designed as a unified security agent, providing a comprehensive secure endpoint experience for users. While its primary and most recognized function is to establish a secure VPN tunnel, AnyConnect extends its capabilities to offer a suite of additional security services. These include features like web security, which protects users from malicious websites; network visibility, giving administrators insights into endpoint activity; roaming protection, ensuring security even when users are off-VPN; and posture assessment, which verifies endpoint compliance before granting network access. This multi-faceted approach ensures that remote devices are not only connected securely but are also protected against various threats. For example, a user connecting from an untrusted network can still have their web traffic filtered and their device checked for necessary security updates before being allowed full access to corporate resources. This integrated security posture is a key benefit of AnyConnect, making it a robust solution for modern remote work challenges. Cisco AnyConnect Secure Mobility Client means anyconnect integrates vpn with web security, network visibility, and posture assessment for comprehensive endpoint protection.. In practical terms, more than just a vpn: a unified security agent.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Cisco AnyConnect supports two primary VPN protocols for remote access: SSL VPN and IPsec IKEv2 VPN. Understanding their differences is key to choosing the right solution for your network. SSL VPNs, which actually utilize Transport Layer Security or TLS, the modern successor to SSL, are highly flexible because they leverage standard web protocols, specifically TCP port 443. This makes them exceptionally easy to traverse firewalls and Network Address Translation, or NAT, devices, as most networks already allow outbound web traffic. This ease of deployment is a significant advantage, especially for users connecting from diverse and potentially restrictive network environments. On the other hand, IPsec IKEv2 VPNs offer robust security and are often preferred for their superior performance and native operating system integration. However, they might require specific port allowances, typically UDP 500 and UDP 4500, which can sometimes be blocked by firewalls. A common misconception is that SSL VPN is less secure than IPsec; however, modern TLS implementations provide strong encryption. The choice often comes down to balancing ease of access with performance requirements and the specific network environment of your remote users. For instance, if you have many users connecting from public Wi-Fi networks with strict firewalls, SSL VPN might be more reliable.

Configuring a basic AnyConnect SSL VPN on a Cisco IOS-XE router involves a structured series of steps to ensure secure and functional remote access. First, you need to enable the webvpn feature on the router, which is the foundational command that activates the necessary services. Next, a critical step is to configure an SSL trustpoint for the router's identity certificate. This certificate is essential because it authenticates the VPN server to the client and encrypts the SSL/TLS control channel, ensuring that clients are connecting to a legitimate server and that their communication is private. Obtaining and installing a valid certificate, either from a public Certificate Authority or an internal Public Key Infrastructure, is a prerequisite for this step. Then, you define a webvpn gateway, which specifies the external interface IP address that clients will connect to and associates it with the SSL trustpoint you just configured. Following this, you create a webvpn context, or webvpn group on older IOS versions. This context defines all the specific VPN parameters for a group of users, such as the IP address pool from which clients will receive their IP addresses, the DNS servers they should use, and the authentication method. Finally, you associate this context with the gateway and apply the webvpn command to the external interface, bringing the entire service online. Each step builds upon the previous one, creating a robust and secure remote access solution.

Let's walk through the initial configuration steps on a Cisco IOS-XE router, focusing on setting up the SSL trustpoint and the webvpn gateway. The SSL trustpoint is crucial because it defines the identity certificate that the router will present to AnyConnect clients. This certificate verifies the server's authenticity and encrypts the initial control channel, preventing man-in-the-middle attacks. You'll typically obtain this certificate from a trusted Certificate Authority, or generate a self-signed one for lab environments. Once the certificate is installed, you configure the crypto pki trustpoint and associate it with the certificate. Next, we define the webvpn gateway. This command specifies the external IP address and port that remote users will connect to, and it links this connection point to the SSL trustpoint. For example, if your router's public IP is 198.51.100.1, you'll configure the gateway to listen on this address, typically on port 443 for SSL VPN. It's vital that the hostname configured in the gateway matches the Common Name, or CN, on your SSL certificate to avoid certificate validation errors on the client side. These steps lay the secure foundation for all subsequent AnyConnect connections.

After setting up the SSL trustpoint and webvpn gateway, the next crucial step is to configure the webvpn context. This context, sometimes referred to as a webvpn group on older IOS versions, is where you define the specific VPN parameters that will apply to a group of remote users. Within this context, you'll specify the IP address pool from which AnyConnect clients will receive their IP addresses upon connecting. This ensures that each client gets a unique, routable IP within your corporate network. For example, you might define a pool like 172.16.100.1 to 172.16.100.254. You also configure DNS servers that clients should use, which is essential for resolving internal hostnames. Furthermore, this is where you define the authentication method, which we'll cover in more detail shortly. A key feature configured here is split tunneling. Split tunneling determines whether all client traffic goes through the VPN tunnel, known as full tunneling, or if only traffic destined for the corporate network goes through the tunnel, while other internet traffic bypasses it. This is configured using svc split-tunnel include or exclude commands. For instance, you might include your internal subnets like 192.168.1.0/24 and 10.0.0.0/24. Finally, you associate this context with the previously defined gateway and enable the webvpn feature on the external interface, bringing the entire AnyConnect service to life. This detailed configuration ensures that clients receive the correct network settings and access policies.
